JSON: Name: br_afs_bi_hexamer_proton_ordering Title: Bond-resolved AFM/AFS combined with path-integral molecular dynamics to determine nuclear-quantum-induced proton delocalization and symmetry-breaking in surface-confined benzimidazole cyclic hydrogen-bond networks Short Hypothesis: Nuclear quantum effects cause proton delocalization in short N···N hydrogen bonds of surface-confined benzimidazole hexamers on Ag(111), producing asymmetric M-shaped force-distance signatures and reduced donor–acceptor distances for those bonds; this delocalization is suppressed when the N···N distance exceeds ~2.8 Å or when the adsorption registry is changed. Related Work: High-resolution scanning probe methods (CO-functionalized AFM/STM) have been used to image intramolecular structure and bright-line features between molecules; site-specific force–distance spectroscopy (line-FS) has been applied to probe local electrostatic contrasts at donor/acceptor sites. First-principles methods (DFT, AIMD) provide adsorption geometries and classical dynamics but neglect nuclear quantum effects (NQEs). Path-integral molecular dynamics (PIMD) and gas-phase studies have previously shown proton/delocalized Zundel/Eigen features for small molecules and water but have rarely been combined with site-resolved spectroscopy on heavier organic scaffolds. Limitations in current approaches include: reliance on imaging contrast without direct spectroscopic confirmation of proton positions; CO-tip bending and probe–sample interactions that complicate interpretation; classical AIMD and static DFT that miss tunneling and zero-point contributions; limited substrate and isotope comparisons for assessing environmental effects; and lack of controlled manipulation experiments linking adsorption registry to collective proton transfer. Abstract: We address the challenge of detecting and controlling nuclear-quantum-driven proton ordering in surface-confined hydrogen-bond networks built from benzimidazole molecules. We combine bond-resolved atomic force microscopy and site-specific force-distance spectroscopy with path-integral molecular dynamics to directly link spectroscopic signatures to proton probability distributions and free-energy profiles. The primary contribution is a reproducible experimental–computational pipeline that (i) discriminates donor and acceptor nitrogen sites via asymmetric M-shaped F(z) responses, (ii) identifies coexisting localized and quantum-delocalized protons in cyclic hexamers, and (iii) correlates adsorption registry changes with reversible collective six-proton transfer and chirality inversion. Expected outcomes include quantitative thresholds for donor–acceptor distances that permit proton delocalization, measurable AFM/AFS observables (peak asymmetry and ΔF differences) that report NQEs, and validated PIMD-derived free-energy landscapes that reconcile spectroscopy with microscopic proton dynamics. This pipeline generalizes to probe NQE-modulated proton order in other surface-confined molecular architectures. Experiments: Samples and datasets: prepare submonolayer benzimidazole (H-BI) on Ag(111) producing isolated hexamers, chains, and monomers; prepare isotopologue 1H→1D benzimidazole (D-BI) identically; repeat deposition on Au(111) for substrate comparison. Measurements: (1) BR-AFM constant-height Δf imaging with CO-functionalized tip at 4.8 K and 25 pm/−30 pm imaging setpoints; (2) site-specific force–distance spectroscopy (F(z)) along apparent H-bond bright lines (line-FS) for all six inter-molecular bonds per hexamer; (3) tip-induced manipulation for adsorption-registry rotation and bias-induced collective proton transfer (CPT) with Δf(V) ramps. Simulation datasets: DFT-optimized adsorption geometries and AIMD (classical nuclei) at 50 K; ab-initio PIMD (8–32 beads depending on temperature) for H-BI and D-BI dimers and hexamers; CI-NEB for classical transfer barriers; force-field LAMMPS-PIMD (ReaxFF-derived) for extended sampling. Baselines: (A) imaging-only BR-AFM contrast interpretation without FS; (B) DFT/AIMD results that omit NQEs; (C) classical force-field MD. Evaluation metrics: Δf(z) peak positions and peak-height differences between N and NH extraction (pN); ΔF = Fmin(NH)−Fmin(N) per bond; fraction of bonds with |ΔF| ≤ 1 pN (non-classical H-bonds); donor–acceptor N···N distance distribution (Å); P(RC) proton probability distributions and free-energy barriers (meV); estimated tunneling rate from barrier and mass-dependent transition-state analysis (s−1); switching voltage for CPT (V). Experimental setup details: CO-tip functionalization, qPlus sensor parameters (f0≈24.5 kHz, k≈1800 N/m), oscillation amplitude 0.5 Å, temperature control at 4.8 K and 50 K for complementary measurements. Comparisons/ablations: (i) H-BI vs D-BI to test isotope dependence of ΔF and tunneling rates; (ii) PIMD vs AIMD vs DFT/CI-NEB to quantify NQE contributions to free-energy profiles and NN' distances; (iii) Ag(111) vs Au(111) substrate to quantify substrate hybridization effects on N' lone-pair orientation and suppressed tunneling; (iv) registry-manipulated hexamer states (ground vs intermediate) to correlate adsorption sites with suppression or restoration of non-classical bonds. Data analysis: statistical aggregation over ≥56 hexamers, significance testing for ΔF distributions (t-test or nonparametric equivalent), and uncertainty quantification for P(RC) via bootstrapping. Risk Factors and Limitations: Tip-induced perturbation: CO-tip bending and probe–sample forces can distort apparent Δf contrast and displace protons, confounding interpretation. Temporal averaging: line-FS integrates over fast tunneling dynamics; transient proton-transfer intermediates may be unresolvable. Substrate-specificity: results on Ag(111) may not generalize to less reactive substrates; substrate-induced electronic hybridization can suppress tunneling and bias conclusions. DFT and exchange-correlation errors: computed NN' distances and barriers depend on functional and dispersion corrections; ZPE corrections may be inaccurate. PIMD computational cost and convergence: path-integral simulations require many beads and long sampling for low-temperature tunneling; limited sampling may misestimate rare events. Isotope labeling constraints: selective N1-deuteration chemistry may produce incomplete labeling or side reactions altering adsorption. Scalability: approach is limited to UHV, low-temperature, and well-resolved molecular assemblies; extension to aqueous or bulk systems is not feasible with the same techniques. Metric sensitivity: ΔF thresholds (e.g., 1 pN) may be sensitive to tip condition and calibration, producing measurement biases.
